title: "Linearity of expectation"
execute:
  enabled: true

The [preceding page](expectation-of-functions.qmd) showed that a nonlinear transformation is ordinarily applied before its expectation is taken. A linear combination has an additional simplification. In a CMUdict pronunciation, total phone count $X$ is the sum of vowel-phone count $V$ and consonant-phone count $C$. Must we derive a new PMF for $X$ before finding its expectation?

We derive the general linearity identity, recover count expectations through indicator variables, and then show why neither result requires [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) among the component variables. Independence would let a joint distribution factor into marginal distributions; linearity needs no such factorization.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-linearity
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
cmu$consonant_phone_count <- cmu$phone_count - cmu$vowel_phone_count

mean_total <- mean(cmu$phone_count)
mean_vowels <- mean(cmu$vowel_phone_count)
mean_consonants <- mean(cmu$consonant_phone_count)
linearity_error <- mean_total - (mean_vowels + mean_consonants)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  all(cmu$phone_count ==
        cmu$vowel_phone_count + cmu$consonant_phone_count),
  abs(linearity_error) < 1e-12
)

c(E_total = mean_total,
  E_vowels = mean_vowels,
  E_consonants = mean_consonants,
  identity_error = linearity_error)
```

[**Linearity of expectation**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties) lets us average each contribution and then add those averages:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[V+C]
=\mathbb{E}[V]+\mathbb{E}[C].
$$

The expected vowel and consonant contributions are `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_vowels)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_consonants)` phones. Their sum is the empirical expected total, `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_total)` phones.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-linearity
#| fig-cap: "Every observed total phone count equals the sum of its vowel and consonant counts. Point area represents repeated count pairs."
ggplot(cmu, aes(vowel_phone_count + consonant_phone_count, phone_count)) +
  geom_count(color = "grey", fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "steelblue") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Vowel phones + consonant phones",
       y = "Total phones",
       size = "Entries") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Stating the general rule

For random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[|X_i|]<\infty$ and constants $a_1,\ldots,a_n$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}[X_i].
$$

For two variables and an added constant, this gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]
=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]+c.
$$

The expectation operation passes through sums and constant multiples.

For a discrete pair $(X,Y)$ with [joint PMF](joint-probability.qmd) $p(x,y)$, the rule follows without
an independence step:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]
&=\sum_x\sum_y(ax+by+c)p(x,y)\\
&=a\sum_x x\sum_y p(x,y)
 +b\sum_y y\sum_x p(x,y)
 +c\sum_x\sum_y p(x,y)\\
&=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]+c.
\end{aligned}
$$

The inner sums recover the marginal PMFs; they do not factor the joint PMF.

## Indicators

An indicator $I_A$ takes value one when event $A$ occurs and zero otherwise. Define $\pi_A\equiv p_{I_A}(1)$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[I_A]
&=0\times p_{I_A}(0)+1\times p_{I_A}(1)\\
&=\pi_A.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p_{I_A}(1)=\mathbb{P}(A)$, this gives
$\mathbb{E}[I_A]=\mathbb{P}(A)$ and links the numeric indicator back to the
[event probability](../foundations/probability-measures.qmd#the-empirical-measure).

We verify the identity with the data-derived event that vowel-phone count equals its empirical median.

```{r}
#| label: cmudict-indicator-expectation
median_vowels <- unname(quantile(cmu$vowel_phone_count, 0.5, type = 1))
median_indicator <- as.integer(cmu$vowel_phone_count == median_vowels)
indicator_expectation <- mean(median_indicator)
event_probability <-
  sum(cmu$vowel_phone_count == median_vowels) / nrow(cmu)

stopifnot(abs(indicator_expectation - event_probability) < 1e-12)

c(median_vowel_count = median_vowels,
  E_indicator = indicator_expectation,
  event_probability = event_probability)
```

## Independence is not required

Vowel and consonant counts are associated across pronunciation entries. Their empirical [covariance](covariance.qmd)—the mean paired product of centered counts—is `r sprintf("%.3f", mean((cmu$vowel_phone_count - mean_vowels) * (cmu$consonant_phone_count - mean_consonants)))` phones squared. Linearity nevertheless holds because it concerns sums and marginal expectations, not products.

The linear rule should not be extended to nonlinear operations. In general,

$$
\mathbb{E}[XY]
\neq\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
$$

That product equality requires additional conditions.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify linearity for the transformed count $2V+C$ using the row values and the component means.
2. Why does the expected total calculation not require independent vowel and consonant counts?
3. Show from the two possible indicator values that $\mathbb{E}[I_A]=p_{I_A}(1)$.
4. Which operation in $\mathbb{E}[VC]$ prevents direct use of linearity?
5. A student claims $\mathbb{E}[VC]=\mathbb{E}[V]\mathbb{E}[C]$ because
   expectation is linear. Which operation has been mistaken for a sum?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The row mean of $2V+C$ is 8.849799, and $2\mathbb{E}[V]+\mathbb{E}[C]=2(2.469213)+3.911374=8.849799$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Linearity applies to sums and constant multiples regardless of dependence, so vowel and consonant counts need not be independent. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Because $I_A$ takes only 0 and 1, $\mathbb{E}[I_A]=0\,p_{I_A}(0)+1\,p_{I_A}(1)=p_{I_A}(1)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The product in $\mathbb{E}[VC]$ is not a linear combination, so it cannot be separated without an additional condition such as independence. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Multiplication is not a linear combination. Factoring the expectation of a
   product requires additional conditions, while linearity concerns sums and
   constant multiples.

</details>

Expectation distributes over sums without requiring independence. Together
with the fact that an indicator's expectation equals its event probability,
this rule lets us derive expected counts from event probabilities. The [next
page](when-expectations-fail.qmd) asks what must be checked before treating any
expectation as finite.
